clue.text: Playful visitor from a South American nuts' home

definitions.text: Playful visitor from a South American nuts' home

parts.words: Playful visitor from a South American nuts' home
parts.note: a visitor in a play, Brandon Thomas's farce, who famously comes 'from Brazil, where the nuts come from'

explanation.surface: A frolicsome guest arrives from the land where certain nuts grow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playful' means belonging to a play: Brandon Thomas's Victorian farce, whose fake aunt is introduced as coming 'from Brazil, where the nuts come from'.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of the farce is a visiting relative impersonated by an undergraduate, said to hail from Brazil, home of Brazil nuts.

clue.text: Whence the ray the goggler sees

definitions.text: Whence the ray the goggler sees

parts.words: Whence the ray the goggler sees
parts.note: the goggler is a television watcher, and the picture tube's beam comes from the negative electrode

explanation.surface: Asking where the beam a staring person sees comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'goggler' is someone goggling at the box: old televisions drew their picture with an electron beam from the negative electrode.
explanation.definitionFit: The negative electrode emits the electron beam in a television picture tube.

clue.text: If one has a row, this has colourful possibilities

definitions.text: If one has a row, this has colourful possibilities

parts.words: If one has a row, this has colourful possibilities
parts.note: the word spells an I alongside a line, and the substance is the base of many synthetic dyes

explanation.surface: A quarrel might lead to a colourful scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' and 'a row' point at the letters I and LINE in the word; the substance itself gave the first synthetic dyes.
explanation.definitionFit: The coal-tar compound was the starting point for mauve and many other synthetic dyes.

clue.text: The member is out of time-to do so at Westminster?

parts.note: a leg is a limb, a member of the body
late means having missed the time

explanation.surface: An MP turns up late for business in Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests a Member of Parliament, but it is a limb. Westminster is where Parliament makes laws.
explanation.definitionFit: Making laws is what Parliament at Westminster does.

clue.text: e.g. Britannia on the waves

parts.note: Britannia was the royal family's sailing vessel, not the figure who rules the waves

explanation.surface: The patriotic figure who rules the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Britannia on the waves' suggests the song, but Britannia was also the royal vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: HMY Britannia was the royal family's pleasure vessel.

clue.text: Something wrong in metal construction?

indicators.note: the letters of in metal are built into a new construction

explanation.surface: A fault in a piece of metalwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'construction' rearranges IN METAL.
explanation.definitionFit: An illness is something wrong with the body.

clue.text: Roman market day when no one is said to eat

indicators.note: no one is said aloud, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: none means no one
dine means eat

explanation.surface: An ancient Roman day of trading when nobody ate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is said' makes NONE sound like NUN; 'when' and 'to' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romans held market every ninth day, called the nundinae.

clue.text: The apparel alone proclaimed this Wells character

definitions.text: The apparel alone proclaimed this Wells character

parts.words: The apparel alone proclaimed this Wells character
parts.note: H G Wells's scientist could be seen only through the clothes and bandages he wore

explanation.surface: Clothes reveal a character from a Wells novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Wells's scientist made himself unseeable, so only his clothes showed where he was.
explanation.definitionFit: H G Wells's novel features a scientist who could not be seen except by his clothing.

clue.text: Significance of the idiot's tale

parts.note: Macbeth calls life a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying zero

explanation.surface: Asking what a fool's story really means.
explanation.walkthrough: Macbeth's speech says life is 'a tale told by an idiot... signifying' this; the clue asks what it signifies.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's line the idiot's tale signifies zero, so its significance is a void.

clue.text: The army's bogeyman

parts.note: Bogey is the officer of the famous military march, and an army officer of senior rank

explanation.surface: Soldiers have a figure who frightens them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bogeyman' is not a frightening figure but the officer in the march title 'Colonel Bogey', a senior army rank.
explanation.definitionFit: The march 'Colonel Bogey' names its officer by this rank, so Bogey is the army man of that rank.

clue.text: They knew how to charge — like the Electricity Board ?

definitions.text: They knew how to charge — like the Electricity Board ?

parts.words: They knew how to charge — like the Electricity Board ?
parts.note: the cavalry unit at Balaclava made a famous charge, and an electricity board charges for illumination

explanation.surface: A utility firm known for its bills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' is both a cavalry attack (Tennyson's 'Charge of the ... Brigade') and a bill for power.
explanation.definitionFit: The cavalry brigade made the doomed charge at Balaclava in 1854.

clue.text: Musical teeth

parts.note: piano keys, once faced with elephant tusk, are called by the same slang word as teeth

explanation.surface: Teeth that can make music.
explanation.walkthrough: Slang calls both teeth and piano keys by the name of the tusk material they resemble or were made of.
explanation.definitionFit: Piano keys were faced with elephant tusk, and teeth are jocularly named for the same white material.

clue.text: Abounding in cats and dogs ?

definitions.meaning: rain falling in torrents, as when it pours cats and dogs

explanation.surface: A place overrun with pets.
explanation.definitionFit: Swarming and pouring down hard are both senses of the word, as in rain coming down in sheets.

clue.text: If single-hearted and not single-headed, she would be a queen

indicators.note: a single letter I sits at the heart rather than at the head, so the I is shifted between the middle and the front

parts.note: reine is French for queen

explanation.surface: A woman who, if wholehearted and not headstrong, would be royal.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards from the queen: REINE (French 'queen') has I at its heart; move that I to the head and you get the woman's name. 'Single' is I, the Roman one.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a woman's name, so 'she' stands for it.

clue.text: It may be not mallet but spade one wields here

indicators.note: the letters of the words not mallet may be something else once rearranged

explanation.surface: In a garden plot the tool is a spade rather than a mallet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' tells you the letters of NOT MALLET may be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A rented plot of land for growing vegetables is where a gardener digs with a spade.

clue.text: Like Peel's view halloo, the ultimate in trickery

definitions.meaning: the huntsman John Peel's cry, in the song, would awaken the dead, as the final trumpet call will
the final trick-taking card played in a card game

explanation.surface: A hunting cry is the final word in deception.
explanation.definitionFit: The song says John Peel's hunting cry would wake the dead, like the Judgement Day trumpet; in cards it is the final winning card.

clue.text: The never-ending "Out of Bounds " ?

parts.note: something without bounds has no end; 'out of' read as lacking and 'bounds' as boundaries gives a word built like 'without boundaries'

explanation.surface: A sign reading Out of Bounds that goes on for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of Bounds' is not a ban but 'having no bounds': boundaries plus the suffix meaning without.
explanation.definitionFit: Something with no boundaries is never-ending, infinite.

clue.text: These chairs were always one short for the party

definitions.text: These chairs were always one short for the party

parts.words: These chairs were always one short for the party
parts.note: in the party game, seats are removed so there is always one fewer than players when the tune stops

explanation.surface: A host never has quite enough seats.
explanation.walkthrough: In the children's party game a chair is taken away each round, so one player is left standing when the tune stops.
explanation.definitionFit: The party game is named for chairs and the tune played while players circle them.

clue.text: Touch-line

parts.note: read as a line that touches a curve, not the edge of a football pitch

explanation.surface: The side boundary of a sports field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Touch-line' suggests a pitch's sideline; geometrically it is a line that touches a curve at one point.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry a straight line touching a curve at one point without crossing it.

clue.text: One of the nearest if not the dearest

definitions.text: One of the nearest if not the dearest

parts.words: One of the nearest if not the dearest
parts.note: near means stingy, so one of the nearest is a skinflint, who is far from dear to others

explanation.surface: A close relative who may not be the best loved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nearest and dearest' suggests family, but 'near' is British for mean with money.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoarder who hates spending is 'near', the old word for tight-fisted.

clue.text: The Himalayan peasant " shouts to scare the —" (Kipling)

definitions.text: The Himalayan peasant " shouts to scare the —" (Kipling)

parts.words: The Himalayan peasant " shouts to scare the —" (Kipling)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank line from Kipling about a mountain villager frightening off a fearsome beast

explanation.surface: A quotation from Kipling with its last word blanked out.
explanation.walkthrough: The blank in Kipling's line is the creature the peasant shouts to frighten away.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's peasant shouts to drive off a fearsome beast, the word missing from the quotation.

clue.text: Greek teacher changes his post

indicators.note: the letters of his post change places

explanation.surface: A Greek schoolmaster moves to a new job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' rearranges HIS POST.
explanation.definitionFit: The paid teachers of rhetoric and philosophy in ancient Greece were so called.

clue.text: This type is on the square

definitions.text: This type is on the square

parts.words: This type is on the square
parts.note: 'on the square' is the Freemasons' phrase for being one of their brotherhood, and the square is their emblem

explanation.surface: Describing someone honest and above board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the square' sounds like 'honest', but it is the phrase Freemasons use of a fellow member.
explanation.definitionFit: Of the Freemasons, whose emblem is the set square and who say members are 'on the square'.

clue.text: The class with a mark of distinction

definitions.text: The class with a mark of distinction

parts.words: The class with a mark of distinction
parts.note: Hindu social classes are shown by a coloured sign painted on the forehead

explanation.surface: A top school form marked out for honours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark of distinction' sounds like an award, but it is the coloured sign Hindus wear on the forehead to show their hereditary class.
explanation.definitionFit: A hereditary Hindu social class, shown by a forehead mark.

clue.text: It keeps a guy down to earth

definitions.text: It keeps a guy down to earth

parts.words: It keeps a guy down to earth
parts.note: a guy is a rope steadying a tent, held to the ground by a stake

explanation.surface: Something that stops a man getting above himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' is not a man but a guy rope, and 'down to earth' is literal: pinned into the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A camping stake holds the tent's guy ropes fixed in the ground.

clue.text: Reactionary heart ?

parts.note: reactionary read as where a nuclear reaction happens, and heart as the core of an atom

explanation.surface: The core of a right-wing diehard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reactionary' is not political: it is the core where a reaction takes place, the centre of an atom.
explanation.definitionFit: The central core of an atom, where nuclear reactions occur.

clue.text: It's not proved that I turned awkward

indicators.note: the words I turned are put into an awkward, ungainly order

explanation.surface: A suspect protests that his clumsy turn proves nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awkward' rearranges I TURNED; 'turned' looks like the anagram signal but is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not yet put to the test is not proved.

clue.text: Hailed as quite a lark on the stage, too

definitions.meaning: Shelley's skylark ode opens 'Hail to thee', addressing the bird as a merry soul
Noel Coward's comedy about a ghostly first wife has the same title

explanation.surface: A comedy show praised as great fun.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelley's ode greets the skylark with these words, and Coward used the phrase as the title of a ghost comedy.
